lesson.title: Loosening and Tightening the Genome's Packaging
lesson.summary: Chemical modifications added to the tails of histone proteins, especially acetylation and methylation, change how tightly DNA is wound around histones and thereby influence how easily a gene can be transcribed.
lesson.body:
DNA in the nucleus is not loose spaghetti, it is wound around spool-like proteins called histones, and each spool of DNA plus histone is called a nucleosome. The tails of the histone proteins stick out from these spools, and those tails can be chemically decorated with small molecular tags. Because different tags change how accessible the underlying DNA is, histone modification is a second major mechanism of epigenetic regulation, working alongside DNA methylation.

Acetylation is the clearest and most consistent case. Enzymes called histone acetyltransferases add acetyl groups to positively charged lysine residues on histone tails. DNA's backbone is negatively charged, so it normally clings to the positively charged histones; neutralizing that positive charge with an acetyl group weakens the grip between histone and DNA. The chromatin loosens into a more open configuration, often called euchromatin, transcription factors and RNA polymerase gain easier access, and gene expression generally goes up. Enzymes called histone deacetylases remove acetyl groups and reverse the effect, tightening chromatin into a closed, repressive configuration called heterochromatin and generally lowering expression.

Histone methylation is less predictable, and that unpredictability is itself an important lesson: unlike acetylation, which almost always opens chromatin up, the effect of adding a methyl group to a histone depends heavily on exactly which amino acid is modified and how many methyl groups are added. For example, trimethylation at histone H3's lysine 4 position is strongly associated with actively transcribed genes, while trimethylation at H3's lysine 27 position is strongly associated with repressed genes. Two chemically similar marks, placed at different addresses on the same protein, can send opposite signals, an idea sometimes called the histone code.

Because the DNA sequence itself is never touched in any of this, histone modification qualifies as epigenetic under the same definition covered earlier, and these patterns can be propagated to daughter cells as chromatin is duplicated alongside DNA during replication. Histone modification does not act alone, though: the physical opening or closing of chromatin that acetylation and methylation influence is finished off by a distinct, mechanical process called chromatin remodeling, covered next.
